REASONS FOR DECISION

[1] XXXX XXXX, the claimant, seeks protection under sections 96 and 97(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA).1
SUMMARY

[2] The claimant is alleged to be a woman of Tibetan ethnicity born in India. She left India in 2003 and sought asylum in the United States. The application was refused. She remained in the United States and appealed the negative decision. She alleges that she is a follower of the Dalai Lama and fears that she would be persecuted on this basis by Chinese authorities if she were to return to India and be deported to China.

[3] The claimant's application was initially rejected by the Refugee Protection Division with reasons dated June 20, 2014. The Federal Court granted the application under judicial review on July 21, 2015, and returned it to the RPD for a re-determination. The hearing was held, I noted the observations of the Federal Court, and these are my reasons for decision stemming from the re-determination. The evidence before me included the documents from the previous RPD hearing, counsel's written submissions from the previous RPD hearing, the transcript from that hearing, the RPD reasons, the Federal Court decision, new evidence submitted for this hearing, written submissions for this hearing, and post-hearing evidence which I allowed as it was relevant to the question of obtaining an Indian passport.
ISSUES

[4] The determinative issues in the claim are countries of reference, namely the claimant's ability to acquire citizenship in India, as well as forward looking harm, and credibility.
DETERMINATION

[5] I find that the claimant is neither a convention refugee nor a person in need of protection.

[6] In support of her personal identity, the claimant provided copies of her Tibetan Green book, a Tibetan birth certificate, and identity certificates indicating her birth in India.2 I reviewed the evidence before me as well as the reasons that were given by the previous member on this point, and indicated at the start of the hearing that I was convinced of the claimant's personal identity and that it was not an issue for me. On a balance of probabilities, I find that the claimant is ethnically Tibetan, born in India as alleged, and accept her personal identity.
Credibility

[7] I found the claimant to be generally credible and forthcoming in her testimony.
Reasonable efforts have not been made to acquire citizenship in India

[8] I have considered the citizenship laws in India, in light of the recent Federal Court case law regarding Tibetans and their ability to acquire citizenship in India.

[9] Noting the relevant section 3(1) of India's Citizenship (Amendment) Act, 2003:
Except as provided by sub-section (2), every person born in India,
(a) on or after the 26th day of January, 1950, but before the 1st day of July, 1987;
(b) on or after the 1st day of July, 1987, but before the commencement of the Citizenship (Amendment) Act, 2003 and either of whose parents is a citizen of India at the time of his birth;
(c) on or after the commencement of the Citizenship (Amendment) Act, 2003, where
(i) both of his parents are citizens of India; or
(ii) one of whose parents is a citizen of India and the other is not an illegal migrant at the time of his birth, shall be a citizen of India by birth. [italics added]3

[10] Therefore, according to section 3 (1) (a), if the claimant's date of birth falls between January 26, 1950 and before July 1, 1987, and she was born in India, then she falls under one of the categories allowing her to have Indian citizenship. Given that the claimant was born in India on XXXX XXXX, 1961, the claimant meets this criteria, and should be granted citizenship on this basis. However, I am aware of the past difficulties that Tibetans living in India have experienced in being recognized as citizens, despite the existence of this law. However, in recent years, there have been some developments in the law, leading more Tibetans to be recognized as citizens in India.

[11] According to the September 22, 2016 decision of the Delhi High Court, "the nationality of Tibetans born in India between 1950 and 1987 cannot be questioned under the Citizenship Act" in response to petitions filed by three Tibetans born in India, who attempted to apply for Indian passports.4 The High Court directed the Ministry of External Affairs and all passport-issuing authorities to process applications for passports of eligible Tibetan refugees, or else be held in contempt of court.5

subthemes.text:
[12] In light of the New Delhi High Court's decision, the Canadian Federal Court of Appeal decision of Tretsetsang provides some guidance on the application of Williams for Tibetan claimants. This was also referenced in counsel's submissions6:
We agree that the test for determining whether a claimant has a "country of nationality" is the control test as set out in Williams. We also agree that the onus is on the appellant to establish the existence of the asserted impediment and that it would result in the appellant not having the power of control whether India will recognize him as a citizen of India and provide state protection to him. In our view, a country of nationality includes a country where the claimant is a citizen and where the claimant may face an insignificant or minor impediment to accessing state protection from that country but may not include a country where the claimant is a citizen and faces a significant impediment to accessing state protection from that country.

[13] The Federal Court of Appeal in Tretsetsang further outlined the requirements a claimant must meet to demonstrate whether he or she would be able to acquire citizenship:
Therefore, a claimant, who alleges the existence of an impediment to exercising his or her rights of citizenship in a particular country, must establish, on a balance of probabilities:
(a) The existence of a significant impediment that may reasonably be considered capable of preventing the claimant from exercising his or her citizenship rights of state protection in that country of nationality; and
(b) That the claimant has made reasonable efforts to overcome such impediment and that such efforts were unsuccessful such that the claimant was unable to obtain the protection of that state.
What will constitute reasonable efforts to overcome a significant impediment (that has been established by any particular claimant) in any particular situation can only be determined on a case-by-case basis. A claimant will not be obligated to make any effort to overcome such impediment if that claimant establishes that it would not be reasonable to require such claimant to make any such effort.7

[14] I have considered the claimant's allegations in light of the requirements in Tretsetsang. Having considered all the evidence, testimony, and the personal circumstances of the claimant, I find that the claimant has not established the existence of a significant impediment to prevent her from exercising her citizenship rights in India, nor has she made reasonable efforts to overcome such impediments, or that her efforts were unsuccessful.8 As such, I find India to be a country of reference for the claimant and, as such, a claim for protection is to be considered against India, with the claimant required to show that she would face a serious possibility of persecution in India, or that on a balance of probabilities, she would be subjected to a danger of torture, or to a risk to life, or to a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment. I further find that she has not done so.
The claimant has not made reasonable efforts to apply for a passport or overcome stated impediments

subthemes.text:
[15] I find that the claimant has not made reasonable efforts to apply for a passport or to exercise her rights of Indian citizenship. I asked the claimant if she has ever tried to get an Indian passport, and she testified that after reaching Canada her lawyer advised her to seek Indian citizenship. She testified that she asked her daughter to look at the internet for possibilities. She testified that her daughter said that a birth certificate was needed along with other conditions that they are not aware of. I asked when this took place, and she said two or three months ago. I asked if she had ever actually tried to apply, whether online or at an embassy or consulate, and the claimant testified that after checking online, she noted that she does not have a birth certificate or the requirements. She spoke to her limited education, and I asked why her daughter could not assist, and she testified that her daughter checked the criteria, which she says she does not have. I was provided with post-hearing evidence, which lists some requirements for an online application, but does not point to an application actually having been made or any outcome of such an application.9

[16] I find that the claimant has not made reasonable efforts. From the evidence before me, the claimant has never actually attempted to obtain an Indian passport. It appears that the closest she has come is checking the requirements of an online application and taking no further steps. The claimant has therefore never had any attempts to obtain her passport or citizenship refused by Indian authorities. I do not find this to be reasonable. Counsel's submissions note that the Indian embassy does not issue passports but gives consular advice. If an online application is proving challenging, I do not find it reasonable that a claimant would not seek assistance, or advice, from the Indian government's representatives in Canada, particularly given that the claimant testified that they had called the Indian consulate to ask about renewing the claimant's Identity Certificate. There is insufficient evidence before me that the one online application that was looked at is the only way to obtain a passport, that it necessarily would have been rejected, that there are no alternatives to explore, or that an embassy or consulate could not provide assistance. Taking no additional steps beyond simply looking at a list of required documents on the internet I find to be unreasonable and insufficient, as it does not substantiate what the authorities' response may in fact be to an application, or to any alternatives that may be available to an applicant.

[17] I find that the claimant's personal circumstances are insufficient to justify the lack of reasonable efforts. I take into account the claimant's limited education and sophistication. However, I note that she has proven herself capable of living in the United States and Canada, pursuing refugee claims as well as appeals and judicial reviews in both countries, has had assistance from lawyers in both countries, was in fact advised by her lawyer to seek Indian citizenship and did not make reasonable efforts to do so, has been assisted by family members, and was able to take steps to obtain such documents as a Non-Availability of Birth Registration from Indian authorities through a friend in India.10 I find that the claimant's personal circumstances are insufficient to justify a lack of reasonable efforts to pursue her passport and citizenship rights given that she has proven herself capable in related matters and reasonable efforts could have been reasonably expected from someone in her position.

[18] I find that the claimant has not established on a balance of probabilities the existence of a significant impediment to exercising her rights of citizenship and, in any event, I have already found that she has failed to make reasonable efforts to overcome such impediments. A particularly significant argument made was that the claimant does not have the documents to apply for a passport, in particular a birth certificate, and therefore will not be able to obtain a passport or avail herself of her citizenship rights. This is a significant point, and I have considered it.

[19] I asked the claimant why she could not try to apply for a passport with her Tibetan birth certificate, and she said that it would not be recognized as genuine. I asked her why she thinks it would not be successful, and she said that even though she is unable to read and write, people who have requested help have said that it would not happen. I find this as insufficient evidence to establish that the presence of a birth certificate issued by Tibetan authorities will necessarily be rejected, or that it presents as a significant impediment, or that reasonable efforts have been made to overcome this stated impediment.

subthemes.text:
[20] I asked the claimant if she could go to court to pursue her citizenship rights and she said no, because her education and background will not let her. I do not find the question of pursuing citizenship through the courts to be determinative in this case as the claimant has not taken reasonable efforts to obtain a passport and her citizenship through more preliminary means, and has not established that she would be unsuccessful and would even have to resort to court proceedings.

[21] The claimant provided a legal opinion letter from a lawyer in India, who represented successful Tibetan litigants in obtaining their Indian passports.11 In the letter, the lawyer indicated that he was asked to provide a legal opinion on whether an individual was likely to be eligible for Indian citizenship. Much of the letter is a summary of the law, and only a portion of the letter is relevant to the claimant's situation. The lawyer concludes, based on the identity documents submitted, that the individual about whom he was writing would likely not be able to acquire citizenship.

[22] I have considered this evidence, but find it insufficient to establish significant impediments or to justify a lack of reasonable efforts. The letter was not written specifically for the claimant, but rather provided as evidence due to similarities to a similar claimant. The claimant did not know this lawyer, nor speak to him. The letter does not address the possibility of pursuing an application with a Tibetan passport, or if any alternatives to the listed documents may be considered. The letter is not definitive in its conclusions, only indicating that "the querist is most likely to fail at the initial stage". However, I do not know the other particular circumstances of the individual about whom the letter was written, and it is uncertain what information this lawyer had. This opinion letter appears to be based solely on the identity documents provided to him by a different claimant, and I find that the claimant has not demonstrated that the conclusions are likely to apply to her.

[23] The Indian High Court has already directed the Ministry of External Affairs and all passport-issuing authorities to process applications for passports of eligible Tibetan refugees, or else be held in contempt of court.12 The documentary evidence is insufficient on the prevalence of passport office clerks at Indian consulates globally refusing to accept application forms for the Indian government to consider, and risking themselves to be held in contempt of the court order.

[24] There has been no formal refusal from any Indian government official for the claimant attempting to get a passport or avail herself of her Indian citizenship rights. Therefore, I find on a balance of probabilities, that the claimant has failed to demonstrate a significant impediment has occurred or will occur, and she has not made reasonable efforts to overcome these impediments. I find on a balance of probabilities, that it is within the claimant's control to acquire citizenship in India and the claimant has not met the onus to show otherwise.

[25] Therefore, given the above findings, I find on a balance of probabilities that India is a country of reference.
There is no well-founded fear of persecution in India

[26] I adopt the reasoning of the previous RPD member as it relates to the claimant's likely ability to return to India, based on her past ability to obtain documents, her family connections in India and her husband's continuing role in the Central Tibetan Authority because I have considered the evidence and find the conclusions to be sound.

I will, however, address one additional point: while there was discussion at the hearing regarding the claimant's husband's ability to help, counsel has indicated a view in her written submissions that this would amount to asking an official to overlook the commission of a criminal offense.

According to the documentary evidence, the Central Tibetan Administration has indicated that those who do not renew their Registration Certificate before the expiration may be denied renewal, although renewals are sometimes still granted on humanitarian grounds.

[27] The claimant indicated that she fears that she would be deported to China if she returned to India, because she has been unable to renew her Registration Certificate, which provides her with the right to legally reside in India as a Tibetan.
She claims to have heard of deportations, but does not have evidence because has not witnessed this happening.

She indicated, however, that she had successfully renewed her documents every year since the age of 17 when she was living there.

[30] Therefore, on a balance of probabilities, I find that the claimant will not be persecuted upon her return to India, and she has not established that she has a well-founded fear of persecution if she returns to India, or that on a balance of probabilities, she would be subjected to a danger of torture, or to a risk to life, or to a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment.

[26] I adopt the reasoning of the previous RPD member as it relates to the claimant's likely ability to return to India, based on her past ability to obtain documents, her family connections in India and her husband's continuing role in the Central Tibetan Authority because I have considered the evidence and find the conclusions to be sound. I will, however, address one additional point: while there was discussion at the hearing regarding the claimant's husband's ability to help, counsel has indicated a view in her written submissions that this would amount to asking an official to overlook the commission of a criminal offense. I do not find this to be the case. According to the documentary evidence, the Central Tibetan Administration has indicated that those who do not renew their Registration Certificate before the expiration may be denied renewal, although renewals are sometimes still granted on humanitarian grounds.13 Therefore, it is at the discretion of the Foreign Registration Office, whether or not an expired Registration Certificate can still be renewed, and it would not be improper for the claimant to attempt to do so, with or without her husband's assistance.

[27] The claimant indicated that she fears that she would be deported to China if she returned to India, because she has been unable to renew her Registration Certificate, which provides her with the right to legally reside in India as a Tibetan. I asked her if she had any other fear of living in India, and she reiterated that it would be stressful since her Registration Certificate has expired, that she does not have other documents to be there, and if authorities find out there is the possibility of being deported to China.

[28] I do not find a serious possibility of harm on these grounds. I have outlined reasons above the claimant's possibility of returning to India, her past success in obtaining documents from authorities, and the possibility of renewing an expired Registration Certificate. I also observe that her ability to live without fear in India might change if she made reasonable efforts to obtain a passport and avail herself of her rights as an Indian citizen, which she has failed to do. She claims to have heard of deportations, but does not have evidence because has not witnessed this happening. According to the documentary evidence, Tibetans are never actually forced to leave India, nor are they handed over to the Chinese authorities.14 Therefore, I find based on the objective evidence the claimant's belief that she would be deported if returned to India to not be a well-founded fear of persecution, and that she would not face a serious possibility of harm of such deportation occurring.

[29] I also considered if there may be any other risk of harm she might face returning to India. I asked the claimant why her husband and children can remain in India, and she indicated that for them the conditions are the same, they have to renew their documents and going for the renewal is a stressful experience. She indicated, however, that she had successfully renewed her documents every year since the age of 17 when she was living there. She has not alleged additional risk of harm as a Tibetan in India beyond this concern over documents, and I observe that her family continues to live in India without evidence of harm. I therefore find insufficient evidence of any additional grounds on which to find a serious possibility of persecution or harm if she were to return to India.

[30] Therefore, on a balance of probabilities, I find that the claimant will not be persecuted upon her return to India, and she has not established that she has a well-founded fear of persecution if she returns to India, or that on a balance of probabilities, she would be subjected to a danger of torture, or to a risk to life, or to a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment.

discussion_units.text:
[3] The claimant's application was initially rejected by the Refugee Protection Division with reasons dated June 20, 2014. The Federal Court granted the application under judicial review on July 21, 2015, and returned it to the RPD for a re-determination. The hearing was held, I noted the observations of the Federal Court, and these are my reasons for decision stemming from the re-determination. The evidence before me included the documents from the previous RPD hearing, counsel's written submissions from the previous RPD hearing, the transcript from that hearing, the RPD reasons, the Federal Court decision, new evidence submitted for this hearing, written submissions for this hearing, and post-hearing evidence which I allowed as it was relevant to the question of obtaining an Indian passport.
ISSUES

[4] The determinative issues in the claim are countries of reference, namely the claimant's ability to acquire citizenship in India, as well as forward looking harm, and credibility.
DETERMINATION

[5] I find that the claimant is neither a convention refugee nor a person in need of protection.
IDENTITY

[6] In support of her personal identity, the claimant provided copies of her Tibetan Green book, a Tibetan birth certificate, and identity certificates indicating her birth in India.2 I reviewed the evidence before me as well as the reasons that were given by the previous member on this point, and indicated at the start of the hearing that I was convinced of the claimant's personal identity and that it was not an issue for me. On a balance of probabilities, I find that the claimant is ethnically Tibetan, born in India as alleged, and accept her personal identity.
Credibility

[7] I found the claimant to be generally credible and forthcoming in her testimony.
Reasonable efforts have not been made to acquire citizenship in India

[8] I have considered the citizenship laws in India, in light of the recent Federal Court case law regarding Tibetans and their ability to acquire citizenship in India.

[9] Noting the relevant section 3(1) of India's Citizenship (Amendment) Act, 2003:
Except as provided by sub-section (2), every person born in India,
(a) on or after the 26th day of January, 1950, but before the 1st day of July, 1987;
(b) on or after the 1st day of July, 1987, but before the commencement of the Citizenship (Amendment) Act, 2003 and either of whose parents is a citizen of India at the time of his birth;
(c) on or after the commencement of the Citizenship (Amendment) Act, 2003, where
(i) both of his parents are citizens of India; or
(ii) one of whose parents is a citizen of India and the other is not an illegal migrant at the time of his birth, shall be a citizen of India by birth. [italics added]3

[10] Therefore, according to section 3 (1) (a), if the claimant's date of birth falls between January 26, 1950 and before July 1, 1987, and she was born in India, then she falls under one of the categories allowing her to have Indian citizenship. Given that the claimant was born in India on XXXX XXXX, 1961, the claimant meets this criteria, and should be granted citizenship on this basis. However, I am aware of the past difficulties that Tibetans living in India have experienced in being recognized as citizens, despite the existence of this law. However, in recent years, there have been some developments in the law, leading more Tibetans to be recognized as citizens in India.

[11] According to the September 22, 2016 decision of the Delhi High Court, "the nationality of Tibetans born in India between 1950 and 1987 cannot be questioned under the Citizenship Act" in response to petitions filed by three Tibetans born in India, who attempted to apply for Indian passports.4 The High Court directed the Ministry of External Affairs and all passport-issuing authorities to process applications for passports of eligible Tibetan refugees, or else be held in contempt of court.5

[12] In light of the New Delhi High Court's decision, the Canadian Federal Court of Appeal decision of Tretsetsang provides some guidance on the application of Williams for Tibetan claimants. This was also referenced in counsel's submissions6:
We agree that the test for determining whether a claimant has a "country of nationality" is the control test as set out in Williams. We also agree that the onus is on the appellant to establish the existence of the asserted impediment and that it would result in the appellant not having the power of control whether India will recognize him as a citizen of India and provide state protection to him. In our view, a country of nationality includes a country where the claimant is a citizen and where the claimant may face an insignificant or minor impediment to accessing state protection from that country but may not include a country where the claimant is a citizen and faces a significant impediment to accessing state protection from that country.

[13] The Federal Court of Appeal in Tretsetsang further outlined the requirements a claimant must meet to demonstrate whether he or she would be able to acquire citizenship:
Therefore, a claimant, who alleges the existence of an impediment to exercising his or her rights of citizenship in a particular country, must establish, on a balance of probabilities:
(a) The existence of a significant impediment that may reasonably be considered capable of preventing the claimant from exercising his or her citizenship rights of state protection in that country of nationality; and
(b) That the claimant has made reasonable efforts to overcome such impediment and that such efforts were unsuccessful such that the claimant was unable to obtain the protection of that state.
What will constitute reasonable efforts to overcome a significant impediment (that has been established by any particular claimant) in any particular situation can only be determined on a case-by-case basis. A claimant will not be obligated to make any effort to overcome such impediment if that claimant establishes that it would not be reasonable to require such claimant to make any such effort.7

[14] I have considered the claimant's allegations in light of the requirements in Tretsetsang. Having considered all the evidence, testimony, and the personal circumstances of the claimant, I find that the claimant has not established the existence of a significant impediment to prevent her from exercising her citizenship rights in India, nor has she made reasonable efforts to overcome such impediments, or that her efforts were unsuccessful.8 As such, I find India to be a country of reference for the claimant and, as such, a claim for protection is to be considered against India, with the claimant required to show that she would face a serious possibility of persecution in India, or that on a balance of probabilities, she would be subjected to a danger of torture, or to a risk to life, or to a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment. I further find that she has not done so.
The claimant has not made reasonable efforts to apply for a passport or overcome stated impediments

[15] I find that the claimant has not made reasonable efforts to apply for a passport or to exercise her rights of Indian citizenship. I asked the claimant if she has ever tried to get an Indian passport, and she testified that after reaching Canada her lawyer advised her to seek Indian citizenship. She testified that she asked her daughter to look at the internet for possibilities. She testified that her daughter said that a birth certificate was needed along with other conditions that they are not aware of. I asked when this took place, and she said two or three months ago. I asked if she had ever actually tried to apply, whether online or at an embassy or consulate, and the claimant testified that after checking online, she noted that she does not have a birth certificate or the requirements. She spoke to her limited education, and I asked why her daughter could not assist, and she testified that her daughter checked the criteria, which she says she does not have. I was provided with post-hearing evidence, which lists some requirements for an online application, but does not point to an application actually having been made or any outcome of such an application.9

[16] I find that the claimant has not made reasonable efforts. From the evidence before me, the claimant has never actually attempted to obtain an Indian passport. It appears that the closest she has come is checking the requirements of an online application and taking no further steps. The claimant has therefore never had any attempts to obtain her passport or citizenship refused by Indian authorities. I do not find this to be reasonable. Counsel's submissions note that the Indian embassy does not issue passports but gives consular advice. If an online application is proving challenging, I do not find it reasonable that a claimant would not seek assistance, or advice, from the Indian government's representatives in Canada, particularly given that the claimant testified that they had called the Indian consulate to ask about renewing the claimant's Identity Certificate. There is insufficient evidence before me that the one online application that was looked at is the only way to obtain a passport, that it necessarily would have been rejected, that there are no alternatives to explore, or that an embassy or consulate could not provide assistance. Taking no additional steps beyond simply looking at a list of required documents on the internet I find to be unreasonable and insufficient, as it does not substantiate what the authorities' response may in fact be to an application, or to any alternatives that may be available to an applicant.

[17] I find that the claimant's personal circumstances are insufficient to justify the lack of reasonable efforts. I take into account the claimant's limited education and sophistication. However, I note that she has proven herself capable of living in the United States and Canada, pursuing refugee claims as well as appeals and judicial reviews in both countries, has had assistance from lawyers in both countries, was in fact advised by her lawyer to seek Indian citizenship and did not make reasonable efforts to do so, has been assisted by family members, and was able to take steps to obtain such documents as a Non-Availability of Birth Registration from Indian authorities through a friend in India.10 I find that the claimant's personal circumstances are insufficient to justify a lack of reasonable efforts to pursue her passport and citizenship rights given that she has proven herself capable in related matters and reasonable efforts could have been reasonably expected from someone in her position.

[18] I find that the claimant has not established on a balance of probabilities the existence of a significant impediment to exercising her rights of citizenship and, in any event, I have already found that she has failed to make reasonable efforts to overcome such impediments. A particularly significant argument made was that the claimant does not have the documents to apply for a passport, in particular a birth certificate, and therefore will not be able to obtain a passport or avail herself of her citizenship rights. This is a significant point, and I have considered it.

[19] I asked the claimant why she could not try to apply for a passport with her Tibetan birth certificate, and she said that it would not be recognized as genuine. I asked her why she thinks it would not be successful, and she said that even though she is unable to read and write, people who have requested help have said that it would not happen. I find this as insufficient evidence to establish that the presence of a birth certificate issued by Tibetan authorities will necessarily be rejected, or that it presents as a significant impediment, or that reasonable efforts have been made to overcome this stated impediment.

[20] I asked the claimant if she could go to court to pursue her citizenship rights and she said no, because her education and background will not let her. I do not find the question of pursuing citizenship through the courts to be determinative in this case as the claimant has not taken reasonable efforts to obtain a passport and her citizenship through more preliminary means, and has not established that she would be unsuccessful and would even have to resort to court proceedings.

[21] The claimant provided a legal opinion letter from a lawyer in India, who represented successful Tibetan litigants in obtaining their Indian passports.11 In the letter, the lawyer indicated that he was asked to provide a legal opinion on whether an individual was likely to be eligible for Indian citizenship. Much of the letter is a summary of the law, and only a portion of the letter is relevant to the claimant's situation. The lawyer concludes, based on the identity documents submitted, that the individual about whom he was writing would likely not be able to acquire citizenship.

[22] I have considered this evidence, but find it insufficient to establish significant impediments or to justify a lack of reasonable efforts. The letter was not written specifically for the claimant, but rather provided as evidence due to similarities to a similar claimant. The claimant did not know this lawyer, nor speak to him. The letter does not address the possibility of pursuing an application with a Tibetan passport, or if any alternatives to the listed documents may be considered. The letter is not definitive in its conclusions, only indicating that "the querist is most likely to fail at the initial stage". However, I do not know the other particular circumstances of the individual about whom the letter was written, and it is uncertain what information this lawyer had. This opinion letter appears to be based solely on the identity documents provided to him by a different claimant, and I find that the claimant has not demonstrated that the conclusions are likely to apply to her.

[23] The Indian High Court has already directed the Ministry of External Affairs and all passport-issuing authorities to process applications for passports of eligible Tibetan refugees, or else be held in contempt of court.12 The documentary evidence is insufficient on the prevalence of passport office clerks at Indian consulates globally refusing to accept application forms for the Indian government to consider, and risking themselves to be held in contempt of the court order.

[24] There has been no formal refusal from any Indian government official for the claimant attempting to get a passport or avail herself of her Indian citizenship rights. Therefore, I find on a balance of probabilities, that the claimant has failed to demonstrate a significant impediment has occurred or will occur, and she has not made reasonable efforts to overcome these impediments. I find on a balance of probabilities, that it is within the claimant's control to acquire citizenship in India and the claimant has not met the onus to show otherwise.

[25] Therefore, given the above findings, I find on a balance of probabilities that India is a country of reference.
There is no well-founded fear of persecution in India

[26] I adopt the reasoning of the previous RPD member as it relates to the claimant's likely ability to return to India, based on her past ability to obtain documents, her family connections in India and her husband's continuing role in the Central Tibetan Authority because I have considered the evidence and find the conclusions to be sound. [29] I also considered if there may be any other risk of harm she might face returning to India. I was provided with post-hearing evidence, which lists some requirements for an online application, but does not point to an application actually having been made or any outcome of such an application.9

[16] I find that the claimant has not made reasonable efforts. From the evidence before me, the claimant has never actually attempted to obtain an Indian passport. It appears that the closest she has come is checking the requirements of an online application and taking no further steps. The claimant has therefore never had any attempts to obtain her passport or citizenship refused by Indian authorities. I do not find this to be reasonable. Counsel's submissions note that the Indian embassy does not issue passports but gives consular advice. If an online application is proving challenging, I do not find it reasonable that a claimant would not seek assistance, or advice, from the Indian government's representatives in Canada, particularly given that the claimant testified that they had called the Indian consulate to ask about renewing the claimant's Identity Certificate. There is insufficient evidence before me that the one online application that was looked at is the only way to obtain a passport, that it necessarily would have been rejected, that there are no alternatives to explore, or that an embassy or consulate could not provide assistance. Taking no additional steps beyond simply looking at a list of required documents on the internet I find to be unreasonable and insufficient, as it does not substantiate what the authorities' response may in fact be to an application, or to any alternatives that may be available to an applicant.

[17] I find that the claimant's personal circumstances are insufficient to justify the lack of reasonable efforts. I take into account the claimant's limited education and sophistication. However, I note that she has proven herself capable of living in the United States and Canada, pursuing refugee claims as well as appeals and judicial reviews in both countries, has had assistance from lawyers in both countries, was in fact advised by her lawyer to seek Indian citizenship and did not make reasonable efforts to do so, has been assisted by family members, and was able to take steps to obtain such documents as a Non-Availability of Birth Registration from Indian authorities through a friend in India.10 I find that the claimant's personal circumstances are insufficient to justify a lack of reasonable efforts to pursue her passport and citizenship rights given that she has proven herself capable in related matters and reasonable efforts could have been reasonably expected from someone in her position.

[18] I find that the claimant has not established on a balance of probabilities the existence of a significant impediment to exercising her rights of citizenship and, in any event, I have already found that she has failed to make reasonable efforts to overcome such impediments. A particularly significant argument made was that the claimant does not have the documents to apply for a passport, in particular a birth certificate, and therefore will not be able to obtain a passport or avail herself of her citizenship rights. This is a significant point, and I have considered it.

[19] I asked the claimant why she could not try to apply for a passport with her Tibetan birth certificate, and she said that it would not be recognized as genuine. I asked her why she thinks it would not be successful, and she said that even though she is unable to read and write, people who have requested help have said that it would not happen. I find this as insufficient evidence to establish that the presence of a birth certificate issued by Tibetan authorities will necessarily be rejected, or that it presents as a significant impediment, or that reasonable efforts have been made to overcome this stated impediment.

[20] I asked the claimant if she could go to court to pursue her citizenship rights and she said no, because her education and background will not let her. I do not find the question of pursuing citizenship through the courts to be determinative in this case as the claimant has not taken reasonable efforts to obtain a passport and her citizenship through more preliminary means, and has not established that she would be unsuccessful and would even have to resort to court proceedings.

[21] The claimant provided a legal opinion letter from a lawyer in India, who represented successful Tibetan litigants in obtaining their Indian passports.11 In the letter, the lawyer indicated that he was asked to provide a legal opinion on whether an individual was likely to be eligible for Indian citizenship. Much of the letter is a summary of the law, and only a portion of the letter is relevant to the claimant's situation. The lawyer concludes, based on the identity documents submitted, that the individual about whom he was writing would likely not be able to acquire citizenship.

[22] I have considered this evidence, but find it insufficient to establish significant impediments or to justify a lack of reasonable efforts. The letter was not written specifically for the claimant, but rather provided as evidence due to similarities to a similar claimant. The claimant did not know this lawyer, nor speak to him. The letter does not address the possibility of pursuing an application with a Tibetan passport, or if any alternatives to the listed documents may be considered. The letter is not definitive in its conclusions, only indicating that "the querist is most likely to fail at the initial stage". However, I do not know the other particular circumstances of the individual about whom the letter was written, and it is uncertain what information this lawyer had. This opinion letter appears to be based solely on the identity documents provided to him by a different claimant, and I find that the claimant has not demonstrated that the conclusions are likely to apply to her.

[23] The Indian High Court has already directed the Ministry of External Affairs and all passport-issuing authorities to process applications for passports of eligible Tibetan refugees, or else be held in contempt of court.12 The documentary evidence is insufficient on the prevalence of passport office clerks at Indian consulates globally refusing to accept application forms for the Indian government to consider, and risking themselves to be held in contempt of the court order.

[24] There has been no formal refusal from any Indian government official for the claimant attempting to get a passport or avail herself of her Indian citizenship rights. Therefore, I find on a balance of probabilities, that the claimant has failed to demonstrate a significant impediment has occurred or will occur, and she has not made reasonable efforts to overcome these impediments. I find on a balance of probabilities, that it is within the claimant's control to acquire citizenship in India and the claimant has not met the onus to show otherwise.

[25] Therefore, given the above findings, I find on a balance of probabilities that India is a country of reference.
There is no well-founded fear of persecution in India

[26] I adopt the reasoning of the previous RPD member as it relates to the claimant's likely ability to return to India, based on her past ability to obtain documents, her family connections in India and her husband's continuing role in the Central Tibetan Authority because I have considered the evidence and find the conclusions to be sound. I will, however, address one additional point: while there was discussion at the hearing regarding the claimant's husband's ability to help, counsel has indicated a view in her written submissions that this would amount to asking an official to overlook the commission of a criminal offense. I do not find this to be the case. According to the documentary evidence, the Central Tibetan Administration has indicated that those who do not renew their Registration Certificate before the expiration may be denied renewal, although renewals are sometimes still granted on humanitarian grounds.13 Therefore, it is at the discretion of the Foreign Registration Office, whether or not an expired Registration Certificate can still be renewed, and it would not be improper for the claimant to attempt to do so, with or without her husband's assistance.

[27] The claimant indicated that she fears that she would be deported to China if she returned to India, because she has been unable to renew her Registration Certificate, which provides her with the right to legally reside in India as a Tibetan. I asked her if she had any other fear of living in India, and she reiterated that it would be stressful since her Registration Certificate has expired, that she does not have other documents to be there, and if authorities find out there is the possibility of being deported to China.

[28] I do not find a serious possibility of harm on these grounds. I have outlined reasons above the claimant's possibility of returning to India, her past success in obtaining documents from authorities, and the possibility of renewing an expired Registration Certificate. I also observe that her ability to live without fear in India might change if she made reasonable efforts to obtain a passport and avail herself of her rights as an Indian citizen, which she has failed to do. She claims to have heard of deportations, but does not have evidence because has not witnessed this happening. According to the documentary evidence, Tibetans are never actually forced to leave India, nor are they handed over to the Chinese authorities.14 Therefore, I find based on the objective evidence the claimant's belief that she would be deported if returned to India to not be a well-founded fear of persecution, and that she would not face a serious possibility of harm of such deportation occurring.

[29] I also considered if there may be any other risk of harm she might face returning to India. I asked the claimant why her husband and children can remain in India, and she indicated that for them the conditions are the same, they have to renew their documents and going for the renewal is a stressful experience. She indicated, however, that she had successfully renewed her documents every year since the age of 17 when she was living there. She has not alleged additional risk of harm as a Tibetan in India beyond this concern over documents, and I observe that her family continues to live in India without evidence of harm. I therefore find insufficient evidence of any additional grounds on which to find a serious possibility of persecution or harm if she were to return to India.

[30] Therefore, on a balance of probabilities, I find that the claimant will not be persecuted upon her return to India, and she has not established that she has a well-founded fear of persecution if she returns to India, or that on a balance of probabilities, she would be subjected to a danger of torture, or to a risk to life, or to a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment.
CONCLUSION

[31] After carefully considering all the evidence in this claim, and for the reasons above, I find that the claimant is not a convention refugee under section 96 of the IRPA nor is she a person in need of protection under subsection 97 of the IRPA.

[32] The claim is therefore rejected.
